newsitem.title: FRANCE: Election? So what?, say army of jobless French voters.
newsitem.headline: Election? So what?, say army of jobless French voters.

text.p: To many unemployed voters, France's parliamentary election campaign looks like a bad movie re-run.

Politicians from the left and right trade blows over their commitment and capacity to tackle record unemployment, but the promises inspire little hope among the jobless ahead of the two-round election on May 25 and June 1.
Voters are, to say the least, confused and appear resigned to the idea that jobs promises ahead of elections are broken once the election is over, whoever ends up governing.

"What difference does it make? Once they get into power for another five years they'll do nothing," says Marie, back on the job hunt at her local employment agency after a two-month stint in a hotel cloakroom.
"I wouldn't mind, but at 50 there are nothing but crappy little jobs and my daughter has to help me out. It's not right for a mother to have to turn to her daughter for assistance."
Many of the other job-searchers at the ANPE employment agency on Rue Belleville, one of the poorest districts of central Paris, share her feelings.
"I've no idea, no idea at all," a young unemployed office cleaner says with a shrug when asked who she thinks offers the better choice.
Her worry is that cleaning companies are demanding people with secondary level school qualifications to clean toilets and dust computers.
JOBLESS TOTAL AT POST-WAR RECORD

Unemployment is running at a post-war record 12.8 percent, those eligible for unemployment benefit pass 3.1 million and the total number without work is closer to four million when those on minimum state assistance are included.
One in four of the jobless is aged under 25 and one in three has been out of work for more than a year.

The impression is that the jobless have seen it all before, that the picture is still blurred and that casting a vote will not set things right. The political leaders themselves admit they are worried about failing to captivate the audience.

"There should be a vote which obliges the government to keep its promises, or it gets fired," said Jean-Luc, a 48-year-old van driver who wants to change jobs but cannot find offers for anything lasting more than a few months.
What troubles him and other voters is a feeling politicians are incapable of changing things, that what they are saying now has been said in the past, whatever the degree of goodwill.

One of Jean-Luc's most recent memories was Prime Minister Alain Juppe's promise when he took the helm of the centre-right government two years ago to make jobs the absolute priority and his request to be judged on his success.
Juppe was confronted with 11.5 percent unemployment when he took over. He said at the time it would be possible to create 700,000 jobs by the end of 1996.
SOCIALISTS PLEDGE 700,000 NEW JOBS
Now Lionel Jospin, leader of the main opposition Socialist party, says he aims to create 700,000 jobs and secure greater job recruitment by reducing the work week to 35 hours from 39.

Jospin is proposing a more traditional left-wing formula of state support for job creation as well as relying on economic growth, while the right argues that growth is picking up and it will create more jobs by lowering tax on wages.
The perception is that neither is really likely to deliver and, at least for the more militant, that street protest will achieve more than a vote.

Many feel that the new mandate which conservative President Jacques Chirac sought for his centre-right allies in advancing the election by nearly a year will not quell the temptation to voice protest through demonstrations or strikes.

The more angry activists would like to see a repeat of the strikes by railway workers and others in the public sector which brought the country to a near halt in late 1995, despite the failure of other protests to generate such momentum since then.

"It's rage, not courage, which has us on the road," says one of the many French activists taking part in the European March Against Unemployment, Precarity and Exclusion", a protest movement heading for Amsterdam from cities across Europe.
UNEMPLOYED FORGOTTEN IN DRIVE FOR EMU
In France, and elsewhere, activists believe that the jobless and the marginalised are simply being ignored in an obsessive drive by government to bind Europe under a single currency.

Yann, a 58-year-old unnemployed sociologist from Toulouse in southwest France, says he will vote in the upcoming election but could never vote further right than the Communist Party, because he believes no one else is genuinely committed to the poor and because it rejects the "financial model" of the European Union.
His views may be more radical than others, but the degree of disillusion is common.
"I'm in favour of Europe," says Jean-Luc. "At least that way my son might be able to get a job in Belgium or in Germany."
